utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning everybody. And good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So all the accused are present. Prosecution today is like yesterday, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. And the Defence absentees, I notice Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Nikolic, Mr. Krgovic. All right. Mr. Jevdjevic, good morning to you and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with your cross-examination, with your testimony, and hopefully finish. That was also my hope yesterday. Before the end of the sitting yesterday, Mr. Josse raised an objection -- made an objection to a question made by Mr. McCloskey which referred to a particular document. We heard submissions on this objection, both from Mr. Josse and from Mr. McCloskey. Our decision is as follows: We find that it is perfectly fine, correct, for the Prosecution to put the question and even further questions based on or with reference to this document. There is, of course, the fact that was raised by Mr. Josse; namely, that contrary to other instances when we had intercepts and the Prosecution brought as witnesses the persons or the operators who were involved in the capturing of those intercepts, this is not apparently the case in the present. Our position in regard is that if that continues to be the case, obviously this will become a matter of a question of weight to be given to the document itself in due course at this stage of our deliberations. So let's continue. I think it's the case of repeating your question, Mr. McCloskey, because the witness I don't think had answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, if I may, I have got a question from the witness and at least two Defence counsels yesterday about the timing of the 12 July intercept. And if I could briefly deal with that issue, I hope it's brief. I think I can bring some of that to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go back to 65 ter 4807 -- 4087, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I want to give you a little background on what I think I had at least forgotten and perhaps, I think, Mr. Haynes and others may have forgotten as well, is that this intercept - and we see the word "izvestaj," pardon the pronunciation, on the top translated as "report." This intercept, like all the print out intercepts that came from (redacted) They are all part of reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had forgotten that that was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, what we learned from the intercept supervisor and others, is that from this place, the operators wrote down their intercepts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Page and line reference, please, if we are going to assert that this particular report that's been put to him as been dealt with in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what he's talking about, I'm sorry. What?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You don't know what a page and line references? I mean the page of the transcript and the line of the transcript. You said that "We have heard from the intercept supervisor." Who is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the name is protected, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we are in private session, aren't we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, a PW number will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I provided that information in an e-mail last night to Defence Counsel, and I can get it again, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the position of the Prosecution that the fundamentally the systems are the same and I think the Court recalls that. And in any event it was witness -- did we get the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's PW-131, but he didn't give evidence about the facility that this report came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem seems to be the following: It's not the -- you mentioned a particular facility or location to the witness, okay, with specific reference to what we are talking about. It's being put to you now, by Mr. Haynes, that if you are referring to the witness that he has mentioned, PW-131, that witness did not operate from the location that you indicated but from a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can argue for a long time with Mr. Haynes about these issues, but I think we recall that the witness was the supervisor for both places, and so my question, my summary, was meant to be he talked about the policy from both places. I think we recall that. And I can just say both places, if that will clear up the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I will go back to my original issue. Give me a transcript reference of what he said that. Because I am not worried about arguing with Mr. McCloskey, I am worried about the witness being misled by this speech being made to him as was made several times yesterday in the form of questions. If it is not the case there has been evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it easy. Which part of the evidence are you referring to, Mr. McCloskey, because that will be everybody's life easier, otherwise we will continue and continue arguing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have a right as Your Honours note to ask questions that I have a good faith belief in. And we heard from multiple witnesses on this point; they were cross-examined multiple times. I was able to last night find the supervisor that talked about both of them, and I actually sent them the areas. It's 28th of November, 2006, page 4641, and there are many people that spoke about this. They were cross-examined at length about it, and I am asking -- I am informing the Colonel that my basic understanding of that and I have every right to do so as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming it's a generic statement without particular reference to a particular part of testimony of this intercept supervisor or anyone else. Let's hear your question, first, and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's my view that we had learned that these intercepts were sent to the intel section of the Bosnian army in reports and that several reports would go out each day, and in those reports there would be one or more intercepts listed by time and date. And so when we see this intercept that's on the page, this is one report of five reports that came to the intel headquarters from this particular site. The first report was dated -- excuse me, is 65 ter number 4113. Then another report was 4114; another report was 4115; this report that we are looking at is 4087; and another report was 1417. Some of those reports had one intercept, some of them had multiple intercepts. And it's also my view that we were told that the date and time on the intercept in these print-outs reflected the actual date and time that they were taken; but the witness made one exception to that, which we may remember, and that was when an intercept was recorded late in the day, perhaps 11.00, maybe midnight that it would take some time to get that intercept typed up from the notebook and sent off to the headquarters. And so sometimes it would have the date of the following day when it was actually taken, the late night of the day that we were talking about. That's an exception. I am sure everyone remembers that. They were cross-examined on it. And -- but, as we are looking at this intercept, we can see that it's not a late in the day intercept. So that's my fundamental understanding of how this worked. And we can go to, briefly, a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What's the question? And we've checked the page and line reference, and the witness spoke about one intercept at Okresanica, so the whole basis of this speech that has been made for now, 16 lines to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let him ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but let him finish. I mean it's not the first time we have had questions going through pages sometime, and we have been very patient. So please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was asked questions by two counsel and a witness. If they don't want answers, don't ask me the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And sir, I don't want to go over all the intercepts in these various packets, but I did see one of them that had Jevdjo on them that I didn't know about before. So I want to give you a chance to take a look at that. It's 65 ter 4115. And the -- as we get to it you will see the top page of this -- and we should -- it should not go out because it does indicate the site. We see the place and we see the date, then we see the word "report," and we go down -- there are several intercept, and we need to go down to the intercept, it's page 2 of the English, and it's at 10.20 a.m. in the B/C/S. So if we could find that one. The time sequence is not always in chronological order, it is my understanding, because sometimes the way they typed it didn't allow for that. So if we can see 10.20 there and you could take a look at it. It says this is 10.20, it should be -- it's the 12th of July. And Jevdjo says: "Listen, I am calling from Srebrenica, Domar." Do you remember who Domar is? I should know that and I've forgotten. Does Domar sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's a question, Domar could be the code name of the 1st Podrinje Brigade or, in fact, of the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And Jevdjo says: "Did you get my telegram?" And it's talking about children and I can't make much of that. Can you make anything of that? Is your recollection -- is that -- do you know if that's you or?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can comment on this conversation although the participants mentioned here are Djevic, that doesn't ring any bells, Djevic, Domar, Centrala Jevca. That doesn't seem to be a conversation I participated in because I can't make head or tail of it. But the report that we now see on the screen is dated as if it had been sent on the 12th of July from the facility -- or from the location that we mentioned just a little while ago. As you spoke quite a lot about this at the beginning of today's session, I thought I would have an opportunity to comment on this part as a witness. If not, what you said will be taken as correct, and I completely disagree with it. Could you please show me the original of that report which you are holding in your hand so that I can see what form it is in, what it looks like, and draw my conclusion as to what this is about. The first conversation that turned up here yesterday and that we finished discussing yesterday is very important. Two crucial sentences are mentioned there which I do recognise and which are part of my testimony, and I wish to explain to everybody here what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we will get to that. I just want to first - before we get to your big response to what I've hold you - is -- have you answered my question? Do you recall this short intercept between Domar and Jevdjo or Djevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was impossible to establish relay communications from Srebrenica. Any expert can provide you with a profile of the terrain, but there is no optical visibility with the Veliki Zep node. Srebrenica is a town in a deep depression. You have probably been there, so there is no chance whatsoever that a communication line could have been established from Srebrenica with this device for me to be able to say, Listen, I am calling from Srebrenica. That's impossible. And the content of this telegram, you, yourself, said was quite unclear to you and I simply cannot connect it with anything I experienced in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like you, please, to let me see the whole of that report because it's very important in my view, especially the part where that conversation is that was seen on the screen this morning but which we finished discussing yesterday. I wanted to thank you today for your correct treatment of me, and ask you if you could give me that conversation for me to see and that list of my unit, of the people in my unit, because it reminds me of men that I would like to retain in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can give you a copy of that for you to take with you, I don't think that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but could you please give me that report with the conversation that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can give you the originals of these five packets so you can study them for the break, but it's not realistic, I don't think now, to give you all the five packets to study while we are waiting. But I have no problem you getting the five packets and taking a good look at them and -- so you can respond more fully if you like, if that meets people's approval. Or we can do it now and take a break.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd also like to ask you in the notebook, that first original, where the intercept is at the location we discussed yesterday which we said we would not disclose, in the original notebooks were the intercept noted down the communication transcribed it, I would like to see what date and time he entered and whether it's consistent with this report which his komandir drafted. And, in my view, it was done on the following day, and we can't see to whom the report was addressed. We can't see who signed it. That's why I am asking to see it. It takes 24 hours to listen in to a communication, and the people who were at those locations testified to this. It's quite logical for a report on intercepts of the previous day be drafted 24 hours later when the entire listening in is completed. And the notebook containing the intercept of yesterday which was also shown this morning would resolve all my dilemmas, provided that those people were very precise in entering this information. Actually I have no dilemmas, but I could probably resolve yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's what the trial is trying to do. And the notebook we learned also, I can tell you, that sometimes the person in the notebook would write down the date, but many times they would just write down the frequency and the time. And so it's not always clear from the notebook what the date is, and I -- and we'll -- I don't think it's perfectly clear from this notebook what the date is, but that's why we have it. That's why Defence Counsel have it. And I don't think there is going to be a real argument over -- over what I just said. I haven't put in the study to determine a date and get it figured out from the notebook. So in any event let me go onto one more intercept that's in this group of stuff, ask you a couple of questions about it, and then you can address your comments to the whole series of questions and what I have put to you as the theory of the Prosecution's case. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you in what you've said. But, Mr. President, I insist to get, while I am here testifying, the notebook. I know you have the original notebooks where the server directly wrote down the time, the frequency, and contents. That content that his commander framed into some report and at some subsequent time sent to someone - and you cannot see to whom he sent it - because in that conversation absolutely it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem. You can have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, it may be no problem to you, Mr. McCloskey, but the thing is this: Are you alleging, Mr. Jevdjevic, that what you are seeing on the screens on the monitor in front of you does not correspond to what is contained in the original? Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because there is one intercepted conversation that appeared yesterday and that was disclosed this morning here at the beginning which absolutely agrees with my memory and with my testimony. And unbelievably so, it corresponds to the minute. In response to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's limit ourselves to that one only. I mean, why waste or lose precious time which we can use to proceed and continue and finish with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I can show him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then show it to him. If you have it here available, let him see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Unless I am misunderstood the witness, he wants to see P4087 again, and the underlying notebook, both of which I know the Prosecution have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One at a time, okay? I understand that. We understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The notebook, for the record, is 65 ter 2315, and the handwritten version of the -- if we could get 65 ter 4087 which is the Badem 385 intercept that the Colonel and we are most concerned about now. And if we could put that one back up on the screen, 65 ter 4087. Could we put the whole thing up there so we can see the whole page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for one of your other questions, you can see that it's addressed to the army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not sent to them. It wasn't sent to them. I think what you said -- what you said is not correct. The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, military unit such-and-such, strictly confidential, some place, and the date; and the report is being sent without any introduction about what its contents are, and there are no indications of whom the report is being sent to. So let us be clear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are crystal clear, sir. We went over that for months in the trial. So I don't think -- I don't think that's going to be a problem for anyone. And let me hand you the original notebook, and it's this one in pencil, it's this 909. You'll recognise the words. You might put it up -- take a look at it and put it on the ELMO so everyone can see what -- what you are looking at and what your observations are. It's page 33 of 2315 that you are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here, and we can show it on the ELMO, that there is no date written anywhere of this intercept, only the time. When you turn a page back, you can see the date 5th of July, 1995, and then you don't see anywhere any dates on the next pages; and then again, which is absolutely consistent with my testimony and with this intercept where it says at 1850. And, according to me, this is absolutely on the 11th of July where I rule out -- where, actually, I turned off the devices at Pribicevac and I had to inform some of the participants for them to know. And then I say, From now on we will be a Badem, extension 385; Badem is Bratunac, this is my intention to go to Bratunac, because according to me Bratunac is some new logical forward command post towards, which Krstic left on the 11th; and this was my thinking. Badem you will get through Zlatar, meaning I am informing some participants about my movements so that they know that I left Pribicevac, and then, according to me, what is crucially important, and I said that yesterday when you asked me precisely to say what time I left Pribicevac, and I told you around 1900 hours. Down, in this sentence, the last sentence, the server, who was eavesdropping on this or listening in on this device simply said, At 1900 hours no carrier signal on frequency 295.850 -- 255.850, which means at that point in time the devices were switched off and the receiver at Pribicevac was not emitting its signal. All of this happened on the 11th absolutely the way I testified eight years ago and throughout these days of my testimony and now. This report was sublimated by the commander of these serves and then sometime on the 12th when all these conversations were listened in to, then they were all put together and they were sent to some intelligence organs of the 2nd Corps. It doesn't say that anywhere, but I agree that. So what I am saying here now is the absolute truth, and it's total consistent with all of my testimony about all the things that you disagreed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. There is one more intercept that was in the view of the Prosecution, that one more report containing -- actually two intercepts, from the 12th. There is one I mentioned. I just want to ask you just briefly ask you about, it's 65 ter 1417. And while we are up here, I can give you a hard copy, just ignore my markings. There is just some highlighter markings above in the top that I don't think anybody should care about. Now, this report of two intercepts was sent out on 12 July. And this first intercept was -- you can see the frequency, it should be an RRU-800, I think. And it's between 1, an officer from Srebrenica; and 2, someone named Raso, and Raso was inaudible so they were only able to hear 1. And I just want to ask you about the third paragraph. It says -- 1 says -- sorry, the first thing 1 says on the second paragraph: "As far as the road is concerned, it is free. I went this evening in that direction and returned at 8.00. I was right there where you can turn to Kravica" -- And I forget to mention this is at 22.00 hours. And then the same guy says, we don't hear the answer from the other guy, apparently. The same guy says: "Well, it is. The one group came across a minefield over here, and about 20 of them died. But anyway, it is very well blocked. In any case, 25.000 requested to go. Did you watch the news? Did you see the boss among Bulas down in Potocari. That was the big strong hold. UN contemplated to declare Potocari and the villages around a safe area but that also slipped from them. Now they can also declare whatever they want, mother fuckers." And then it goes on and talks about some other things. As we scan through it, to be fair, I don't know if there is anything you want to talk about in there. Do you have any comments on any of the rest of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no intention -- well, I don't know, I would like to help you also to not to use so much time and not to read this enormous text to the end, but what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Doesn't this help date this particular intercept because they are talking about the time that the Serb forces were able to take the stronghold of Potocari? And we all know that happened on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, believe me, for me more or less on the basis -- from all of this what the most relevant thing is what the servers wrote in their own hand in the notebooks. When, at what point in time, their commander had time, and when he assessed that some information should be summarised and sent to someone in the form of a report. For me, this is a piece of information with less relevant facts; and this question of yours to me is something that I cannot rely on anymore, and I cannot speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this is here is the frequency of the RRU-800 device. It's a completely different device. The connection was intercepted along a different direction and with different technology in comparison to the intercepts that we commented on previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That has pretty much --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That document wasn't on any list, and we have had three lists in relation to this witness now. We have had a list for cross-examination, amended list, a second amended list, and a third amended list at 8.30 this morning. That document wasn't on it. Are there any more that the Prosecution are going to use that we don't know about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he'll check his e-mail, he will find that it was originally numbered as 4116, but we found that it was already in evidence at 1417. This material was all sent out last night when I endeavoured to answer their questions and find this material to help with the date issue. It was sent out all last night. Ms. Stewart was able to get it out on to a list this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, that has pretty much finished my questions on this issue. So if -- and you were able to give, I think, much of your views. But if you have any further views on this, now is the time, but try to be as precise as you can be - if you have any other further views. But Mr. Haynes will be able to ask you questions and so you will be able to talk to him as well, but you can always explain any of your answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my answers so far have been made. Thank you for allowing me to do this. What I want to say again is that when you look at this report that you have given me, definitely other than some contents, other than the meat on it, there is nothing it that we can relevantly claim that it's a report. It doesn't state anywhere what period of time is covered with these intercepts, when they were intercepted. It doesn't say to whom the report is sent, who drafted it, there is no signature of the drafter. So I am now in a position -- or I simply am in a position mostly to believe the notebooks which were directly written into -- although, you can see in them that the server did not write a single date from the 5th of July onwards. But I do recall my conversations, and they all exclusively relate to the 11th of July at the times referred. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. One last intercept and this relates to the question -- questions or question you got regarding - I believe it was an intercept - and correct me if I am wrong, my memory is beginning to fade - but between General Gvero and someone on the 23rd of July regarding, I believe it was the western front, or that was the interpretation of the intercept. Now, we were provided collections of intercepts that the Croatian government gave us, and the Defence has had access to those, and I can't recall if perhaps the Miletic team may have shown you some of those. But I just want to ask you about of those that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 4110.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the reason I am asking you about that is it mentioned General Gvero on the 23rd of July. But before we put that up there, can I ask you, you were involved in the Zepa operation, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, go ahead and put it up. Basically from the beginning to the end, I think you said you had gone back to the Drina Corps Command maybe once. But if you could blow that up a bit so the colonel can read it. I have got a hard copy Colonel, if you -- it's a little tough to read. Now, in the Croatian intercepts that we had, this -- they seem to be more of a synopsis than the question and answer that we were used to seeing from the Bosnian 2nd Corps. But basically we can see that from this synopsis the people that took this said: "An unidentified user who today, 23 July 1995, escorted General Gvero during his inspection of the front line near Zepa regarding this situation of the enclave, said the following: 'From the beginning of the Serb attack on Zepa, 17 soldiers were wounded, including two of them from today. The advance of Serb forces is stopped currently at the bridge head and railroad tracks.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simple question, do you recall General Gvero ever inspecting the front line troops, especially near -- you know, near or on 23 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I am also responding to the previous question. I am hearing for the first time that you have the intercepts available provided to you by the Croatian government. So General Miletic's Defence did not inform me about those documents, but I am trying to more or less analyse each document. And, for example, what strikes me forcefully is this last sentence, "The advance of Serb forces is stopped currently at the bridge head and railroad tracks." The bridge head is the land feature that you would capture by crossing the river in -- using the available means and then the unit would reach the opposite bank and enables the entry of the rest of the forces and that is the bridge head. That whole area only has one little small creek call the Zepa, it's a small, tiny river called Zepa; it's not on the map. And this other expression, "railroad tracks," absolutely there was never any railroad or railroad tracks there. And so the conversation or the information out of that context here -- well, close to Sarajevo there is no railway tracks, and Sarajevo is at least 100 kilometres away from Zepa. So this is not clear to me, I cannot help you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the part about wounded soldiers. Does that sound right? It says, "Up until today" -- it says, "17 soldiers were wounded, including two of them from today, the 23rd."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have wounded soldiers in the Zepa operation, probably also some soldiers were killed, I don't remember the specific numbers. But this is quite usual data when you are waging war. It's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Thank you very much. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And thank you for your professional conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know that there is going to be re-examination, and I know that the Chamber normally likes re-examination to take place before any requests for further cross-examination, but, Your Honour, I wish to ask a few questions about that intercept to help the Chamber as to what I wish to ask about. If the Court goes to page 29650 of the transcript, which was the 12th of December, in the middle of that page there was a question from Mr. Ostojic to this witness about intercepts, and I simply want to apply that test to this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. I think it's appropriate he should ask about this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just consult -- yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Nor do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Josse. Mr. Petrusic, I take it you are fine with having Mr. Josse put these questions before your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you to my learned friends. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Jevdjevic, in relation to that document that is no longer on the screen, could we put back there please 4110. You have got your own hard copy of it. I want to ask you, as I have already said, on the 12th of December of this year, when Mr. Ostojic on behalf of Colonel Beara was asking you questions, he went through what he described as several key elements that one needs to look for in relation to a particular intercept. And I want to ask you about those as far as this document is concerned based on the information that we have got. First of all, the azimuth, does the information that we have there help us in regards to that at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The frequency?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The channel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The directions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The participants?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can see that the last two are fulfilled; namely, does tell us something about the date, the time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. So, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document P2670, please. Can we scroll the document down so we can look at the bottom of the page in the Serbian version. That is page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, in the course of yesterday's testimony the Prosecutor showed you this document from the command of the 1st Podrinje Brigade. At the bottom in handwriting, it says, "Delivered at 1400 hours." Based on this note, are you able to conclude that the telegram was delivered at the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to see 5D1412 please. Could I see the last page in the Serbian version, please. That's the last page in the English version, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were also shown this document which was issued by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and is entitled, "Plan for programme of the course for sniper shooter in the army of Republika Srpska." And at the end there is a stamp, can you tell us whose stamp this is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the department of the military security service in the command of the 5th Corps, or department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the 5th Corps -- or, rather, when the 5th Corps was given its name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Corps was established in 1997, sometime in February or March, and I was the first chief of communications in that corps. Before that I had been a brigade commander in Sekovici for a year. And as I testified, even while I was brigade commander, I didn't get any orders for training for sniper shooters and the 5th Corps was established in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, was that previously the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it comprised the Sarajevo Romanija, Herzegovina and Drina Corps. It was a new formation established in 1997 in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing this document anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, several times in the course of your testimony you said that you had made a statement to the OTP and that you testified in the Krstic case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the investigator of the OTP. I gave that statement in April 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The event you describe concerning the 11th of July and the -- your departure from Pribicevac, is it identical in the statement you gave to the OTP as to your testimony in the Krstic case as regards the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you made that statement to the OTP in April 2000, did you have any contacts with the Defence of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that would be all. I have no further questions. Just a moment, please, excuse me. Yes, I am finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jevdjevic, good morning first of all.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will begin with that part of the Prosecutor's cross-examination which refers to the testimony of witness Velo Pajic on the 26th of November, 2008. A part of this testimony was read out in the courtroom, and if you recall that's transcript page -- it's dated the 25th of September, 2008.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel repeat the line, pleases, and the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Pajic, with reference to the part of that transcript, was on the 26th of November, 2008. Page 28841, lines 22 to 23. He told you or he read out to you that Mr. Pajic stated that on the 0764 line, the frequency was 783, on that route. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I listened to the tape with Mr. Pajic's testimony, and I will read to you what he said about that in his own language, in B/C/S: "Now the transmission and reception frequencies were determined, the number of the transmission frequency, let's say 783, on the route 0674, in 1993, that number was the same in 1995. That means the frequencies were not changed when the transmission was, let's say, 783." Let me tell you right away that the Prosecutor read out correctly the English text of the transcript. The Prosecutor did not make a mistake. The mistake is in the interpretation. The witness said three times the word "recimo," "let's say," which was not interpreted. Could you please explain how you understand this word which Mr. Velo Pajic used when he said that the frequency was "let's say 783"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he only wanted to give an example to illustrate either to the Prosecutor or to you how frequencies were determined. This word, "let's say," can be used as a synonym for the words "for example." So he was just giving an example. He wasn't saying what the precise frequency on that route was. I was very surprised when I heard the Prosecutor say that because he was an exceptionally good signalsman. So I was surprised that he would have some other sort of information from the information that the Chief of Staff had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day, the 15th of December, the Prosecutor also told you that most of the intercepts were intercepted from this frequency, 783. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that that frequency was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's on became 29715, line 24 to 29716, line 2. And now there is no error in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at 1D321, please. That is Mr. Rodic's finding. Page 20 in the B/C/S version and 24 in English. I have just been informed that only the English version is on the screen, but it doesn't matter because there is no text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will see that these are just numbers. In the first column of the intercepts and in the second column, the ERN numbers, as we call them here, those are the numbers under which they are registered in the Tribunal's database; and in the third column are the frequencies from which these alleged intercepts allegedly originate. So please pay attention to the third column, or, rather, the last one, where the frequencies are mentioned. And pay attention to frequency 783, and tell me how many intercepts can you see here as originating from frequency 783?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That frequency isn't mentioned in this list at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next page, please. I would like to ask you again to look at the last column and tell me how many intercepts you notice on this page originated from frequency 783?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That frequency is not found in this list, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have one more page, that's the next page. It's a little shorter. So, again, please tell me on this page how many intercepts originate from frequency 783?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That frequency is not found here, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Jevdjevic, the Prosecutor showed you this intercept dated the 12th of July, 1995. I think it's 4087, but I missed it now. You know what it's about. It's that very brief report, and you were interested in when that conversation was recorded and whether the date from the report corresponds to the date when the conversation was intercepted. I will try to assist you in that, and I will tell you that there is a notebook dealing with that. I think it was admitted into evidence when Prosecution Witness 130 was testifying, and that was on the 6th of December 2006. And the part I am going to read to you now, which refers to the reports, is on page 5078, lines 2 to 12. I will read you what it says in the transcript: [In English] "Tell me please, I did not quite understand yesterday your answer to the Prosecutor's question in relation to entering dates into the computer. Could you tell me whether that date was automatically typed into the computer or did it actually have to be typed out by the operator who was transcribing the text?" Answer: "Well, in the morning when a report would be made for the previous day, it would be sufficient if we would report to the command in the morning. That's when the date would be entered." [Interpretation] We won't read that text any further. Can you tell me, please, how you understand from these explanations, because these are operators who were or are entering information into this notebook, what you understand to be the date of the report and the date of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand from this that the report was dated a day later than the day when the conversation was intercepted, and this is fully consistent with what I stated at the beginning of today's testimony without knowing what you just read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, let's look at this Prosecution exhibit which was shown to you this morning, that's 4115. And let's look at the first conversation recorded here -- or, rather, the last one, excuse me I misspoke. The last conversation on this page. Assuming that you were actually a participant in this conversation, you'll see it's very brief. The first question is: "What's new?" J. says: "Nothing, everything is great. And we expect in two or three days everything will be ours." Can you tell us, it follows from this -- I think this was on the 12th of July, I think it says that up here at ten past 10.00. Can you tell me, if you remember that you really did engage in this conversation, how do you understand this phrase, "Everything will be ours"? What could that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't think of anything concrete. Let me just read the whole conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it continues on the next page. Of course, if you can provide us with an explanation, if not --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if for technical reasons we could take the break ten minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you think you will be cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would hope to do it in one standard session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jevdjevic, you're on the home straight now. With good luck and a following wind, we should be done before the afternoon. I want to start, please, by just reminding you of some of the questions you were asked by Mr. McCloskey by showing you a document, which is 65 ter P2894. As with all documents, please take your time to familiarise yourself with it, but do you recall being shown that document by Mr. McCloskey when he was asking you questions a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's a document that's authored by General Zivanovic and concerns, as it were, instructions to Legenda whom we know is Major Jovovic, bad pronunciation. He was the commander, we he not, of the so-called Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I use the phrase "so-called" advisedly. That was, in fact, a nickname for the unit, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of unit were the Drina Wolves and do you know what their technical name was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the Podrinje Detachment of Special Forces, and I think they later became one of the battalions. But they were part of the Zvornik Brigade as one of the regular units of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you part of the Drina Corps when that unit was created?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just approximately can you help us as to when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not established right away. I think it was sometime in 1993, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now going to show you another document, 7D1089, and this is a document I am going to need your help with. And to be fair to you, I am going to give you a hard copy for you to look at. Now, the reason I am going to need your help with this, Mr. Jevdjevic, is there no English version of the document at the moment. So I'm going to ask you to read it quite slowly for the interpreters. Firstly, can you tell us what sort of document it is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the command of the Drina Corps from the time stated here, which orders the units to carry out certain organisational and establishment changes in their composition in line with the establishment books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know about anybody else, but I don't appear to be receiving any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am, too. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. It was my jack plug wasn't pushed in far enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I see, all right. If you look at the transcript, I think you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the paragraph I would like you to read to us slowly enough for the interpreters to follow you is paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The motorised brigade [as interpreted] of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade remains in the establishment composition of the same, but it is to be kept in the books as a maneuver unit of the command of the Drina Corps under the direct command of the corps. Bring the battalion up to manpower levels, up to a hundred per cent, according to the personnel and material establishment. It has the role of a complete battalion, which may be strengthened with units at platoon and company level from the OMJ anti-aircraft defence and artillery units. "The battalion must have personnel who are relatively young, experienced, and the most fit and able to carry out combat tasks. The strength of the battalion may be between 500 and 900 men with establishment equipment. This battalion is to be reformed, brought up to manpower levels, and organised as the first unit of the professional army of Republika Srpska. And for its formation, bringing up to manpower levels, training, and fitness, ask for help from the command of the Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we scroll down a little, please, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if you could kindly slow down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Jevdjevic, I think we can stop there. To what unit do you understand this order to refer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the command of the Drina Corps, establishing a unit. The motorised battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, this refers, in fact, to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But which battalion in particular does it refer to? It said it is a maneuvers battalion, the first unit of the army --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that refers to the motorised battalion of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's not beat about the bush, does this refer to the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were colloquially called the Drina Wolves, so the wolves from the Drina. That was a unit that was established in compliance with this order. I remember that, and they had their barracks in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is meant by the phrase, "under the direct command of the corps command"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit participated in almost all the operations carried out by the Drina Corps and in almost all the operations where the Drina Corps sent its units to say area of responsibility in other war theatres, and it means that the Drina Corps had the role of commanding that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you were asked some other questions by Mr. McCloskey about P29. So if you can just see that, briefly, to remind yourself of the document I am talking about. Again, Mr. Jevdjevic, just familiarise yourself with it in your own time and tell me when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it necessary for me to read any of the paragraphs in particular? Are we going to be discussing them specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recognise that as Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It states that it's from the Main Staff, and the Directive 4 is being sent to the Commander Chief of Staff personally, probably the corps are involved, but I didn't have the opportunity to see these documents, neither did I know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as a military document, would you describe a directive as strategic, operational, or tactical?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a strategic level document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why it did not ever reach me. It couldn't have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about the brigades, would a strategic document such as a directive be sent to the commands of the brigades within the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of a unit at the level of a regiment or brigade. These documents do not reach units of that level, regiment brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now please have in e-court P0329 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this is another document you've seen before. I think I might have called the wrong document up into e-court, here. Nope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: P3029, that's P329. I recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this is the Drina Corps order to the Zvornik Brigade on the basis of Directive 4 sent to the Zvornik Brigade on the 24th of November of 1992. Is that the document you've got in front of you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one of the initial phrases in this document, "personally to the commander or the chief of staff." Does that mean that the document would be given to the commander if there was one or if there was not to his chief of staff and deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know how many commanders the Zvornik Brigade had in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is immediately after the forming of the Drina Corps, and I personally went to the Zvornik sector to take the RRU-800 device there and to set up communications with them. And I recall that their first command in that period was in the Orahovac elementary school for a while, after that they looked for other locations. There was an old lieutenant-colonel there. I could remember the name if somebody mention it first. His deputy was Captain Dragan Obrenovic, whom I knew very well. And at that time, until the forming of the Drina Corps, or, rather, until General Pandurevic came, there was a time when at least a few commanders replaced each other in a very short period of time. So I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We know in this case that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic became commander of the Zvornik Brigade about a month after this document. So it doesn't appear it would have been delivered to him personally. Do you know yourself who was the commander in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an old lieutenant-colonel, but throughout that who whole time the Chief of Staff was Captain Obrenovic, and he remained the Chief of Staff of that brigade when Pandurevic came to that sector. I am practically certain that the person who issued the order knew about the problem there, that there was no permanent commander and that is why he probably either put the Chief of Staff there because it's very unusual to address it -- to address a document either to the commander or the Chief of Staff personally you knew -- you had the opportunity to see that for yourself on a series of documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll move, and in fact we'll move on a few months to the beginning of 1993 when I think we can all agree that Vinko Pandurevic was both the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and engaged in combat activities outside his area of defence together with you on a number of occasions. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think another commander was a person who was seriously wounded in the stomach, a major, he came from Sarajevo front; and I cannot believe how it is that I cannot remember his name right now. But I think I gave a lot of answers already. His last name was Petkovic, Petkovic, Petkovic. Before him there was another old lieutenant-colonel and this Petkovic was seriously wounded in the stomach in these combat activities at the time, and he hails from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just focussing on, as it were, the initial paragraphs of the document that's in front of you. Did the Zvornik Brigade have in military responsibilities in relation to Visegrad, and if so to your knowledge what were they in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not its area of responsibility, the Visegrad section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: My fault, bad question. Did Vinko Pandurevic have any responsibilities in command of a unit in relation to the area of Visegrad in the early part of 1993 and did it relate to the dam?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when war began in that area, Vinko Pandurevic came with a battalion. But I believe that it was in 1992 -- no, actually, I don't believe it was in 1993. It was in 1992. There was a large thermo-electric power station built in Visegrad of 1992 of 350 megawatt capacity and the Muslim forces from Visegrad in 1992 -- in the spring of 1992, captured the dam, took up -- occupied the dam. They placed explosives there and they threatened to blow up the dam thereby flooding the whole of Visegrad and endangering all the towns that were along the river Drina, including Zvornik, Bijeljina, and so on and so forth. And I know that Pandurevic came, he was probably captain-first-class with of a battalion of either the Uzice Corps, I assume that, and he successfully solved the problem. And he informed the barracks up there that was in Visegrad earlier. If this reflects what you were thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It does, thank you. You were also asked by Mr. McCloskey about your knowledge of any involvement Vinko Pandurevic may have had at Kamenica. And with respect, the questions were left hanging in the air, as if there was something deep, dark, and suspicious involved. Can we have a look at what did happen at Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I would have put into e-court, please, 7D1006, please. And can I just say for everybody's benefit, the underlining in paragraph 2 occurred in my office, I am sorry to say. This happens from time to time, lines get put on documents, so that was not on the original. But it appears to have been replicated in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you read paragraph 2 to yourself, please, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Our units focussed on fortification of the achieved lines and preparation for the forthcoming operations establishing the 4th -- the line of the 4th infantry battalion, line trig point 599, Breznik, and in depth, some village." "Then continual ambush in the Star Selo, Crni Vrh sector. Surveillance and reconnaissance and monitoring of enemy movements. Next, an interview was conducted with a Muslim who was captured yesterday in Krizevici, but no significant information could be obtained. It was decided to send him to the village of Kamenica, with 'the statement of the Zvornik VRS command' offering the Muslim people, children, women, and the elderly, that they can safely depart from the territory of combat operations. "A corridor shall be provided through which they can move without fear ..." Probably that's the corridor Glodi, Kamenica, Redzici, Samapi, Brezik, Cepik, Caparde, Vijaca [phoen], Crni Vrh, to Kalesija and Tuzla. "... because in this manner we wish to prevent unnecessary innocent casualties. The corridor is opened from 0700 hours, to 1700 hours every day." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you've read that and had the opportunity to refresh your memory of what happened in Kamenica in 1993. Do you recall that accommodation made by Vinko Pandurevic in relation to that combat?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that he opened a corridor for women, children, the elderly and the innocent could leave in order to avoid unnecessary casualties. I did hear of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, having considered that and given your earlier evidence which I don't think was challenged about Ustipraca, I am going to have -- ask you to look please at certain rules which applied to the army at the time. And I would like you to look please at P409. And to cut matters short, I think we will just look at point 80, which is B/C/S page 32 English page 33, because many of the other rules have already been put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you like me to read so that I could comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would just like you to remind yourself, by which I don't mean read out loud regulation number 80. So if you take just a moment or two to read that, I've got two very short questions to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. You were asked by Mr. McCloskey on certainly one occasion, but possibly more than one, to comment on the legality of certain documents or actions. In the light of reminding yourself of that regulation, would you express your view as to the legality of Vinko Pandurevic's behaviour at Kamenica, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It accords with Article 80 of the rules, and he even made it a little bit more difficult for himself because he secured the corridor regardless of the fact that there might have been armed people there even though it says here if the bombardment in question would endanger or make uncertain the military operation concerned. So he opened the corridor regardless of this it possibility, and it was open every day from 0700 to 1700 hours. What I am saying is that he might have jeopardized the outcome of his own military operation in order for the civilians to leave that theater if they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And similar comments to what you witnessed at Ustipraca, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's absolutely the same situation. And simply General Pandurevic was such an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, moving on a couple of years, you were the communications officer in relation to Operations Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica 95. Can you now recall when you first learned that Vinko Pandurevic as commander of the Zvornik Brigade had allowed the 28th Division to walk to freedom to Nezuk through a corridor at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I had that information some time towards the end of our operation, specifically that a corridor was open. Not a lot of information about this in Zepa, but I don't know if it was on the basis of intelligence data that a corridor was opened. According to the same principle, more or less, to reduce casualties. And Obrenovic personally told me that he had at his disposal the entire brigade artillery and anti-anti-aircraft guns, Pragas, to combat that column. But for some reason they decided to open the corridor and for that column to pass. I know that he had an agreement about opening the corridor with the commander of the other side, a certain Semso Muminovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And hearing that Pandurevic had done that, did it surprise you knowing him as you did as a man and as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't surprise me. The only thing was that I was concerned that that level of self-initiative is something that the superior command may not tolerate since in this last instance what was involved was armed column of the 28th Division which was conducting a regular military action, and that is the withdrawal from the theater. So I left open the possibility that he personally would be reprimanded or punished because of the column, because he knew it consisted exclusively of armed men who were taking all the available possibilities, taking advantage of all the available possibilities, and there was an option that they might have an all-out battle against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, thank you for that. We are going to move on, now. I want to see if I have understood correctly how a communications centre works at an operational forward command post. Does it work as an extension to the corps command's main switchboard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had that at the IKM, the communications centre at the IKM had an extension and was the only one to be able to get in touch with the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the number 385, firstly, was that used both at Pribicevac and Krivace?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And secondly, I simply don't know the answer to this, was it always used as the forward command post extension number by the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During those two operations in Krivaja and Stupcanica, definitely, I know that. I am not sure whether we had that same number in 1993 let's say, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the extension in existence during the period of time, whenever that was, between the closure of one IKM and the opening of another?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the technical aspect it doesn't make any difference. It's the same as if the switchboard in the apartment where you live assigns you a number and then gives your neighbour another number; and since it doesn't mean anything to you if you go from one operation to another. It's possible that it was a different number earlier. I cannot be clear, but the principle is absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yet again, to see if I've understood it correctly, it's a radio communication via the transmitter at Veliki Zep, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a radio relay connection, to be specific, and in all cases from the beginning to the end of the war, it's same relay connection using the same devices through the Veliki Zep communications node. We can allow for the possibility that earlier there was a different extension, perhaps, but from a technical point of view it didn't mean anything or from the point of view of organising and functioning of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So did it work a bit like a modern mobile telephone; namely, when it's switched on you can receive calls but when it's not you can't?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, but the devices were switched on throughout the duration of these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just like a modern mobile telephone, it can receive both, as it were, voice communications and text communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can send oral and written information through the device. I am talking about the air RRU-1 radio relay device for communications from the IKM to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for those who are very adept with modern mobile phones, just like that, you can send information to multiple recipients, can't you? You can send text messages to an address book?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objects object to leading, we are really getting into different technologies here and dangerous territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey is right, Mr. Haynes. I am sure you can move faster on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So between the period of time when the communications centre at Pribicevac was closed down and the communications centre at Krivace was established, what would happen to encrypted telegrams or messages in written form which were sent to the extension number of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telegrams remained at the communications centre of the dispatcher. They would pile up and wait for the time when the communications with the receiving end would be established so that they could be dispatched. If, for example, the deadline was -- had expired or was close to expiry because of the urgency of some telegram, then the server at the communications centre had to inform the person who was seconding the telegram about that. But in the briefest terms, the telegrams would pile up at the dispatcher's communications centre, then you would wait for the connection to be re-established with the receiving side, and then these telegrams would be dispatched to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Was signal strength ever a problem with a communications centre at a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well was there ever an interruption in the signal or the loss of a signal?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no interruption or loss of signal. Occasionally, we would have brief difficulties while sending the telegrams, but we never had any problems in the transmission of oral communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us in detail about three separate actions in which you ran a communications centre. And I'm going to deal with each of them very briefly. In relation to Operation Mac, you told us that you originally set up a communications centre at Trnovo but that it did not remain there, it move to Lubardici. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this place is called Lubardici, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Forgive me, my pronunciation improves but will never be perfect, I suspect. Why did it move?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it's a logical military action, which I described. The communications centre moves when the forward command moves, and the forward command post follows its units so as to be at an appropriate distance for purposes of observation and successful command. The forward command post moves and then the communications centre moves with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did the removal of the command centre from Trnovo to Lubardici require any written order from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a daily need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In relation to Operation Stupcanica 95, you told us that after a few days the communications centre moved from Krivace to Godjenje. Was that for the same reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it moved to the village of Godjenje, and towards the end of the operation to trig point Zlovrh, without any written orders because it's a logical military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does a mobile communications centre at a forward command post actually amount to? What is it in physical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a truck, quite simply, with a cabin. The truck is on wheels, that's why it's called "mobile," and the exclusive purpose of this is to be able to make fast leaps and bounds following the combat disposition, to follow the combat disposition and the forward command post at an appropriate distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In your view, is a truck with some communications equipment on it synonymous with a command post within the meaning of the rules shown to you by Mr. McCloskey yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while we're on the subject of command posts, who is the first person you would expect to find at a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person who has to arrive is someone from the staff command to set up tents, tables, an ops room. Very soon these people are followed by signalsmen, comms men, to set up communications, which is why I went there a day ahead of Krstic. When all this is ready, the commander arrives to the forward post, at the forward command post. That's the logical military sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what determines when a forward command post moves, or who determines when a forward command post moves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post moves according to need, but it's up to the commander to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just remind ourselves, where was General Krstic on the 11th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, he was in the village of Krivace -- sorry, Pribicevac, until the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did he go then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then, together with General Mladic and General Zivanovic, in two separate vehicles, he left for Srebrenica. To the best of my knowledge, he went to the command of the Bratunac Brigade from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know where he was in the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening of the 11th of July, he was in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and he attended the meeting I spoke about at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other meetings he attended that night?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Was there any reason on the 11th of July to continue having a communications centre at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just remind us, what is at Pribicevac, what physically is there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pribicevac is and was a place where there are clearings in the woods, some meadows and some cottages. It's a small scattered mountain village which had been previously inhabited by Serbs, and then cottages were razed to the ground, burnt down.
