So now it's mountainous terrain with woods and clearing in the woods and meadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what men would have been tied up in the continued manning of a communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A simpler question: Who was present at the communications centre before you packed it up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there and six of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what sort of men are they? Are they ordinary soldiers or are they men with some technical ability?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were ordinary privates, one of them was also a driver as well as being a signalsman. They were just ordinary privates who had been with me through part of the war. And in my view, they were able to respond to the tasks I assigned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How would you have gone about communicating with General Krstic in Bratunac during the evening of the 11th of July had you remained at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been almost impossible. I would have had to have been a magician. I could have tried to find him through various communication centres, through couriers, but the task would have been almost insurmountable to reach General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just one other point on this topic. You were shown some documents which had been either sent or received by the forward command post which had been marked by hand. And Mr. McCloskey drew a distinction between those which had apparently been marked with a "1" and those which had been marked with a "2." Do you recall being shown those documents or would you like me to show you an example of them again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to what someone wrote in handwriting at the top of the document, then I know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good, then we can save some time. Just to confirm what you said to Mr. McCloskey, those markings were not in your writing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you have any idea what they indicate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, probably that was a number in command logbook, when those telegrams were being accounted for after the operation had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that a process you had anything to do with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that the two numbers indicated different communications centres. But can I ask you this: How many combat operations did you take part in in the month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of July, I participated in two operations, Krivaja and Stupcanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when were the written orders for Operation Stupcanica 95 signed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just going back to something we were discussing earlier. In order for a telegram to arrive at the forward command post - have I got this right? - it's important that you know the right extension number?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of how the telegram is addressed, does that matter as long as it's sent to the right extension number?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever addressed the telegram to someone probably was unaware of the technical means used to have that telegram reach the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to show you one document to illustrate the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's P2085. And can we start, please, by showing the witness the second page, the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to give you the floor on this one, Mr. Jevdjevic. The stamp and the handwritten information at the bottom of that document, what does that tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stamp is the stamp used when this document was entered into the logbook of the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. And the date on it is the date when it was entered into their book, the 14th of July it appears to be?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can see it's addressed to the Drina Corps IKM-1. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- at that time, the Drina Corps throughout this period had simultaneously or, rather, had only one forward command post at the time. That's what this marking means. Had there been one in Pribicevac and one in Sekovici, they would have been called IKM-1; that would have been Pribicevac; IKM-2 would have meant Sekovici. As throughout July and throughout that period, the Drina Corps had only one forward command post at a time. That meant that forward command post. I don't know what the date of the telegram is. It's illegible, so I can't tell where we were at the time at Pribicevac or at Zepa, but that's immaterial because it simply implies the forward command post where we were. I am saying this even before seeing the date because that's how it was. If someone has the original, maybe they can assist me and help me see the date, but it was sent to the forward command post. Whether it was at Pribicevac or at Zepa, that's what IKM-1 means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That was really the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we could help if we just went to the end of the document and he can clear that up where I think it is legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, would you have a look at the end of the document again and see whether there is anything you can help us with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said at the outset. This is the seal of the logbook of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, so that's the date, the 14th of July, when the document was entered into the logbook under the number we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that probably doesn't take matters any further forward. I am going to leave that behind for now. Now, you were asked a number of questions yesterday afternoon and this morning about one particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I am going to ask now, please, that we have in e-court P4087. And that the witness be provided again, please, with P2315, the handwritten intercept notebook number 231. And the page ERN number is 7909 that I want him to start at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's in e-court, but I don't think his will be marked the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just a few simple questions, Mr. Jevdjevic. Do you have in front of you the page which has written in handwriting a conversation which is said to involve Major Jevdjevic and the switchboard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is there any date on that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If you go backwards in the book, what is the first date you find?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the conversation. Previously several such conversations were recorded and the first date back is the 5th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many pages are there in that book between the 5th of July 1995 and the conversation which is in this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one page, that's this one. And half of the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know if you think you are able to do this, but how many conversations does it appear to you are recorded between the 5th of July of 1995 and the conversation that is the subject of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 5th of July to this conversation where I am mentioned, only five conversations were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just looking at those conversations, do any of them contain the words, "Titanik, Atlanta, Vezuv, Central," or any numbers? In simple terms, Mr. Jevdjevic, can you find the conversation that's at the top of the report we've got?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this notebook here, which I think the original, there is no record of a conversation mentioning Titanik, Atlanta, Vezuv, and some five digit numbers in between. But -- well, it's included here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've been given a lot of information about evidence you were not here to experience, but do you have any understanding yourself of the process of monitoring radio communications made by enemy armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know quite a lot about that because in the JNA, in the 1980s, there was a whole branch of the army that was established called electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activities, and as this branch is very similar to the communications branch all the personnel in that branch initially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt the witness, but since he's on this topic, perhaps he could move the book forward in time from the key conversation to see what the next date is, if any, and then the explanation may have more meaning and save me some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am perfectly happy to do that, but in seven hours of cross-examination, if you have failed to ask questions you want to ask. Please go forward and tell us what the next date in the book is, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jevdjevic, if you flip over, you could tells perhaps what the next date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean the other -- the other way, from the 5/6 -- 5/12, see what the next date is right after the conversation in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, what's the next date after the 5th of July in that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go up, can't see the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, he can answer the question, can't he? We don't need to see the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next date is the 13th, and that's been entered here a few pages later. So between the 5th and the 13th there is not a single date entered. Everyone can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of writing this record down, is it your understanding that this was written in realtime or was, as it were, the subject of a study of a tape recording?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He doesn't really have the ability to answer that, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your microphone's not on. Can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. Let's leave it in the hands of the witness, and he can perhaps tell us -- yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't hearing anything, and it was because I had my microphone on as well. I'm sorry. I will leave this, but it seems to me when the witness was treated to a very long speech about the process of recording these intercepts, it's only fair to him that he should have the complete picture. Now, we can agree that -- how this document, this written document can came to be, or I can ask him whether he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, we don't want any speculation from you. If you know, you know, if you don't, you don't. But if you know, you also need to tell us how you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I completed the military academy, the communications stream, and the same personnel were used to man the arm of service dealing with electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activities. And that's why I am so familiar with this, and that's the basis of my knowledge and why I can talk about it. All conversations are intercepted on certain channels of transmitters. And when a soldier who is intercepting a conversation hears someone speaking on a certain frequency, he immediately switches on the tape recorded which we used to refer to as "uher," and he would record that conversation. He knew that it was a military channel. After several conversations had been taped, when the soldiers were finished with their shift, they would take those tapes and listen to them again after the lapse of a certain amount of time, and then they would transcribe them in these notebooks. So the data here is correct, but it was transcribed after the conversation was actually recorded. Then they would give these transcripts to their komandir, their commander, who would then compile a report. So they tried to listen into a conversation, then they would make an arbitrary decision as to whether the conversation was important enough to be recorded or whether it was purely personal in nature and, therefore, need not be recorded. That was how it happened in practice on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did they, to your knowledge, have any information as to when midnight had passed and another day had commenced upon them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've looked at the small conversation at -- that is recorded in the second part of the report. Is this a conversation that sitting here now you actually recall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so. It's completely logical to me. I remember and I testified about this yesterday that when I wanted to switch off the devices at the Pribicevac IKM, I informed the other participants about it so that they could know and not to call me at that location anymore because I would not be there anymore, and where I would be next and where -- to which section I would be moving. And that is why yesterday I found this intercept so important. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I now am not receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think it's my jack plug this time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not receiving interpretation. So Mr. Jevdjevic, I think you need to start all over again and hopefully we will get interpretation this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How far back to we need to go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just we started the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't get Mr. Haynes's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Getting a sense or hear or understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What date did that conversation take place, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was conducted on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of his answer previously he added something previously which was not translated which was triggered by Mr. Haynes's question. So what did you say at the time? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This conversation was conducted on the 11th of July, at 1850 hours, and just before I said that, I believe it absolutely, I believe the people who intercepted the conversation. It was intercepted precisely at this time as stated here. And at the bottom, the sentence that is very important is that at 1900 hours there is no carrier signal or frequency 255.850, which was the one that I used because the one who wrote it down wrote it down as a very important piece of information which indicates that he no longer had anyone to hear at that frequency, that no signals were being emitted which means that the device was switched off. And this happened on the 11th of July at 1900 hour, which is what I told the Prosecutor yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just before we completely depart this issue, we've heard in this case from your brother, I think his name was Marinko. Was he in the army of Republika Srpska in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname like you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he was the commander of the anti-terrorist company in the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His nickname is also Jevdjo, but he is not a participant in these communications because he never used these devices. These are units that use exclusively Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Now, when it army of Republika Srpska entered the town of Srebrenica on the 11th July 1995, what was your view as to the status of Operation Krivaja?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to belabour it. Did you think Operation Krivaja 95 had been completed when the -- when General Mladic and his commanders walked into the town on the evening of July the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not consider it to be completed because we still had not defeated the armed formation of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. It just relocated and regrouped in the northwestern part of the enclave. Until General Mladic at the meeting did not say that tomorrow everyone should go to Zepa, I thought that we would still have major fighting there with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When operations are concluded, irrespective of your views of it, what do commanders customarily do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders come back -- or they go back to their home garrisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you think on the 11th of July there was a need for the commanders to meet?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's essential to conduct an analysis, to debrief, to see what had been done, and then to get to some kind of corrected decision which would then be followed by other assignments. That is what is essential whenever a task is being executed. At the end, to go over it again, analyse it, and to issue the next assignments to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on a separate point, was the taking of Srebrenica a significant event for the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Something to celebrate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, yes, in military terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Give us your opinion of General Mladic. Would you describe him as a patient man?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For professional reasons, I would ask not to answer such questions. But General Mladic was a very authoritative commander and an impulsive one. He made decisions very quickly. He would issue them very curtly and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, excuse me, he insisted that they be carried out without any talking back. That was the kind of commander he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will put this to you for your comments, was he the sort of man that was likely to wait either to celebrate the taking of Srebrenica or to give further orders to his tactical forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he personally wasn't up to any kind of celebration. He very briefly conducted an analysis and immediately issued orders to his forces to regroup the following day to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The commanders of the units of Tactical Group 1, how many of them were in Srebrenica town centre in the early evening of 90 -- July the 11th of 1995 to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was passing myself through Srebrenica, I didn't see any of our soldiers in the town itself. Our units remained at the reached positions. Some closer to the entrances to the town, some farther away. I literally passed through an empty town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you either in preparation for this trial or your previous testimony seen the trial video?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, I saw the video footage when in the town itself General Mladic, Colonel Trivic, and General Krstic met up, General Zivanovic also, and probably a few other soldiers. And then, after that, this was followed by lightening-quick command of General Mladic in his style, And now let's go straight to Potocari, straight to Bratunac; and after that when I passed through Srebrenica around 1900 or 2000 hours at that point in time there were no soldiers of ours in Srebrenica. I am thinking about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you also aware that on the evening of the 11th, General Mladic and General Krstic were at the two meetings at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see something of those meetings in clips via the television monitors. And that was that they had some meetings where representatives of the Muslim authorities from Srebrenica were present as well as the representatives of UNPROFOR. So I know that only in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know where the Hotel Fontana is in relation to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hotel Fontana is in the centre of town, the town of Bratunac; and the command of the Bratunac Brigade at the time was located in the administrative building of a company, Kaolin company; so there is a certain distance between those two locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long would it take even to walk between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a 15 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did General Mladic generally walk anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the front he did have a habit of moving around on foot, but in Srebrenica, in such situations in town I never saw him walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. And just remind us, what time it was that you got to the command of the Bratunac Brigade on the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived between 2100 hours or -- and 2130 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until approximately 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us at the meeting that Vinko Pandurevic stood up and protested about Mladic's plans to go on to Zepa. In a nutshell, what were the principle reasons voiced by Pandurevic for not going to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle reasons were of a purely military nature because he said that the situation was that we still had not cleared that part of the front in terms of the final defeat of the forces of the 28th Division and that they were expected to try to break through in the Kasaba-Konjevic Polje section towards Tuzla and that this could create problems with major consequences. And he, if I can put it that way, in a roundabout way told General Mladic about this problem so that it was not literally a protest; but in that kind of gingerly language he did come out with this problem that evening that General Mladic had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the state of the information available at that meeting as to the whereabouts of the forces of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all knew at the time that they were mainly concentrated in the northwestern part of the enclave, and that it was their intention to go to Tuzla. But when Mladic spoke the sentence after addressing -- the address of General Pandurevic, regardless of all the things that you said, Tomorrow we will all be footing it to Zepa, I thought that he had some additional information that the rest of us did not because he had decided so quickly for a military action that could carry considerable amount of risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to show you a couple of documents, please, about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have P1103 into e-court. That's A in the English, B in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, will we be needing the notebook anymore?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Actually, a thought has just occurred to me. The notebook was put on the ELMO, wasn't it? Is there any reason to protect that information that may have been broadcast? I hadn't intended it to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will see, I will see if there were some initials. I don't think there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, how much longer do you think we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We are getting to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, because we have been an hour and a half already. Do you think you will finish in the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will take had a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if you don't mind, I just want to recap on one small issue before we go on, and I wonder if we could just have back into e-court P4087, which appears to be on the screen anyway. Certainly, the Serbian version is on the screen. Thank you very much. Just two issues about this. You told us about your understanding of how operators worked in listening posts, but I just wanted to see if you could identify for us how many processes are involved in the creation of a document like P4087?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that is just time consuming and he's not really qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll move on. I've got another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about it typefaces and whether they matched up or not. The document in front of you, particularly the document in your own language, is that typeface at all familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the Roman -- or Latin alphabet, probably typed on a computer keyboard or printed on the computer printer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have available to you in 1995 this sort of printer that could produce a document like that? It appears to be a matrix printer, if nobody minds me suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have printers like this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could that document, in your view, have been printed in 1995 in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, not in the JNA. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We know it wasn't. So you've confirmed that. Now, just before the break, we were dealing with the information available to you at the meeting of the 11th of July. Was there any information at that meeting as to the whereabouts of the commanders of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not in the information where the commanders were but where -- or what the location was of the bulk of the forces of the 28th Division. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think something is going wrong. We are getting no translation and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Counsel needs to wait for the translation in English to be completed before beginning his question in English because it's on the same channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Did you get that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It came through encrypted telegram rather than by oral communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and try to conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: My fault, Mr. Jevdjevic, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were in the middle of telling me what information there was or not as to the whereabouts of the commander of the -- commanders of the 28th Division. Can you complete your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This precise information about the location of the commanders of the 28th Division was not something that I had. I don't believe others had it. We just knew in which area the bulk of the forces of the 28th Division were regrouping and what the bulk of the -- or what the main intentions were of the forces. That was something that we had over our surveillance communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We are still not getting communication through the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did get translation, so is it the ... is it the jack again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I think we might have a problem here, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And my next question was -- my technical assistant has just helped me out. My next question was, was there any information about an immediate threat to Serbian settlements at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us you arrived at Bratunac at about 9.30. About what time did you pass through Potocari on your way there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just getting dark, so I think it was about 2100 hours or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you passed through Potocari, did you see any buses?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Any forces of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just a few in small groups of two or three. The majority were in their base which was to the right-hand side looking from the direction that I was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where were the civilians that you saw? Were they on the road or were they behind the fence which we know to be the United Nations compound?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large enough civilians were on the road and around the road along that entire section that I was passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the evidence we have heard in this case suggests that on the evening of the 12th of July, civilians were being bussed away from Potocari. You didn't see anything like that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you are talking about the 11th. In the interpretation what I got was the 12th. I didn't see any of that on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have P438 into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that was shown to you in your cross-examination. I want to show you it to you for rather different purposes. It's an order from the Drina Corps to block the forces of the 28th Division dated the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the second page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as you told us, the second page of the document shows the time it was send, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was 2230 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 2230 hours and 2250 hours when it was dispatched to the other parties that it was intended for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, at 2230 on the evening of the 11th of July, 1995, I think we can all agree that General Zivanovic was still the commander of the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And his dispute and chief of staff was General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But this document is signed by who?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by Colonel Pedrag Jocic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you tell us where General Zivanovic and General Krstic were at 10.30 on the 11th of July such that neither of them were able to sign this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic was sitting at the head of the table to the left of General Mladic, and General Krstic was sitting to the right side of General Mladic at the meeting in Bratunac that I also attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you've told us something else, again, about which you weren't challenged, that a man called Bajagic arrived at the meeting you attended with a big fish for a meal. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we are clear, is fish an appropriate food to eat on a fast day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the meeting occurred, you say, on a fast day before what festival?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the major Christian feast day, St. Peter's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what would you eat on St. Peter's day itself, would it be fish or something else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before St. Peter's day is the last day of the major fast. And on St. Peter's day itself, all the Christians go to the church. They come home, and then they eat food that is not -- that doesn't contain a lot of fat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to show you 7D1086, please. Now, I don't suppose you read English do you, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am going to have to help you with this. This document is a Serbian Orthodox calendar for July 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I could probably stipulate to a lot of the religious stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can stipulate that the festival of St. Peter was the 12th of July, 1995, then we can move on. And one further stipulation, the 12th of July was a Tuesday in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem, and I think it's in the record about four places. But no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, both. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on, please, to people who you recall or you suppose were at that meeting that you attended. Can you tell us who Svetozar Andric is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svetozar Andric is now a general. At the time he was a colonel, and he was the commander of the Sekovici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he take part in Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically whether he was at the meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later he confirmed to me, and I recall, that most of the commanders were there. I think only Colonel Blagojevic was not there, and this is why I didn't want to specify. But later when I spoke with General Andric, he was at that meeting, and he recalls all of the information that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction to one answer of the witness regarding the fast food and food that is appropriate on the day of the holiday, what the witness said that on actual St. Peter's day itself, the food that they were permitted to eat would contain meat and fat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we learn something new every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am told that Tuesday was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That may well be correct. The next document in e-court was intended only to establish the day of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have in e-court please 7D1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this was an interview conducted by Mr. McCloskey who sits to your right with Svetozar Andric in February 2002; and I am going to read it to you because I am not sure that you have it in front of you in your own language. Mr. McCloskey said to him: "We have very reliable sources that say there was no meeting on the 11th, that the meeting was on the 12th. And, General, think about this before you answer the questions, because you got into trouble last time. We have General Mladic, General Krstic, and many other officers on video in meetings most of the evening of the 11th of July at the Hotel Fontana, and I have other reliable VRS officers and soldiers who tell us that the meeting was on the 12th. We know what General Krstic said, he said the 11th, but no one believed General Krstic. But I'm not God. You were there. It's your duty to answer the question as best you can." Svetozar Andric replied: "As far as I can remember, I think that that was on the 11th in the evening." And Mr. McCloskey asked him: "So you could be mistaken, it could be on the 12th?" And he said: "According to my estimation, according to what I have in my head, I think that was on the 11th. Because on the 12th we had a meeting at the Vaga area, Viogor, so I think it was on the 11th, but I have to tell you." Now, do you know Svetozar Andric?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of a man is he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, he became the chief of staff of the corps, and after the war he became the commander of one of the two corps of the army of Republika Srpska; and that tells you all you need to know about that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason he would have to be untruthful in talking Mr. McCloskey about the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions that were put to me and the suggestions put to me reminded me of what Investigator Ruez asked me two and a half years ago, and I gave him the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: By the date of this interview, General Krstic had already been tried, convicted, and sentenced. Can you think of any reason Svetozar Andric might have to try and align his account with General Krstic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have 7D1092 into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can save time and go down a little bit more in that interview where it asks whether there was a meal at that meeting? Yes, I think we only have the one page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I think there is another page, because I seem to have read it. I think it goes over at least one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could counsel verify the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can agree that he was asked whether there was a meal and he said "no" and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fine, let's move on. Can we go to 7D1092 while we're on the subject of meals which was just on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for this material to come up on the screen, I do apologise, but at the meeting nothing was eaten. The fish arrived after the meeting when we had got up to leave and I didn't even taste it. Nothing was eaten during the meeting, the food arrived when the meeting ended and I rushed out through the door. I just glanced at the food, but I didn't have time to eat it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, and we need to go to paragraphs 5 and 6 of this which is a 92 bis statement which has been served on everybody in relation to Zvonko Bajagic. Just reading that to yourself, Mr. Jevdjevic, do you know Zvonko Bajagic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of a man is he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a fervent believer, and he assists many churches and monasteries. He has anyone commended by Patriarch Pavle. He has a large house in Vlasenica, and he is a highly respected eminent householder there. He put himself at the disposal of the Drina Corps as a person who had contacts, and he worked in the rear to help with logistics quarter master supplies with ammunition, fuel, whatever was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason he would have to be untruthful about the date at which he brought a fish to the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's move on, please. Do you know who Momir Nikolic is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I. Although Zvonko Bajagic says here that the officers came to dinner after the meeting. We didn't eat anything in the course of the meeting. Mladic would never have allowed that. But I know who Momir Nikolic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to this, but this will be opening the door to much of what else Mr. Nikolic may have said on these topics and related topics, and I'm not sure we need to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes doesn't seem convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am not sure it's opening any doors. Momir Nikolic was on the Prosecution 65 ter list, and they decided to abandon him. I am not sure in those circumstances what use they could make of anything he might have said on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Clearly he will be opening the door to this, going through this kind of material that he could have led in his direct examination. He's going to be opening the door to me completing the picture on Momir Nikolic, a key player on this. And he wants to do that I will make my motion when it's time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you see Momir Nikolic on the night of the 11th of July of 1995 when you were at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you aware that he pleaded guilty on the 7th of May 2003 and entered a plea agreement with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How is this relevant at this point in the examination? I mean, we all know these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey is questioning the relevance of these similar questions, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were a witness in the trial of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you aware that he said in evidence in his own defence that this meeting that you referred to took place on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with General Krstic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Jevdjevic, I don't know because to this day nobody's been good enough to put the suggestion clearly to you, neither Mr. Ruez nor Mr. Harmon nor Mr. McCloskey; namely, whether it is suggested that you are a liar or mistaken. So let's explore both possibilities, shall we. Sitting here today as a witness in this case, do you have any reason not to tell the truth about the date of the meeting you attended at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As you've already told us a number of times, in April of 2000 you were interviewed by Jean-Rene Ruez, the Prosecutor's main investigator in this case. And I get the impression you recall that quite clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at the time had you had any contact with General Krstic in the sense that he had asked you to be a witness in his Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In April of 2000, did you even know that Vinko Pandurevic had been indicted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In April of 2000, did you have any reason not to tell Jean-Rene Ruez the truth about when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you tell him the truth in April of 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what day did you tell him you attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of July, 1995, at a meeting which began at around 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you recall that in the course of that interview after a lot of questioning, Mr. Ruez eventually accepted that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He insisted trying to jog my memory and convince me that it had been the 12th. Then I asked him quite simply on what basis he was asserting that. I asked him when the evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica began, I remember that very well and one can find that there. He said on the 12th. And I said, Excellent, I wasn't there then. I was already at Krivace. I am absolutely certain of that. He challenged this many times asking me what road I took to Bratunac and so on, but I always remained certain it was on the 11th which is why I was so anxious today when this intercept turned up which confirms this to demonstrate that it does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I am not necessarily going to put another exhibit into e-court, but if anybody wants to check that it's 7D1093 at page 39 in the English. Now in November of 2000 you gave evidence in the trial of General Krstic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you tell the Trial Chamber then that you had packed up your communications centre and attended a meeting at Bratunac on the 11th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that you, in fact, attended, as a witness in the trial of General Krstic, on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were cross-examined by Mr. Harmon twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you shown many of the same documents by Mr. Harmon that you were shown by Mr. McCloskey during the course of this trial?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you make the same observations about them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to assert that that meeting was held on the 11th, that I left the forward command post on the 11th, but at the time I did not have the most precise answers as to how those documents could have been created. But mostly, it all boiled down to what I said today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The teleprinted documents that Mr. McCloskey says that he's going to have analysed at this point in time, they were put to you eight years ago were they or eight and a half years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that could mean a lot of document, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it was only just a very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you may not understand the terminology, Mr. Jevdjevic, but the first time you attended as a witness in November of 2000 was during the Defence case. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the second time was after the Defence had concluded its case and the Prosecution had produced some more evidence and then you were recalled by the Defence about five months later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following year in the spring of the 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this might be stretching your memory a little bit, but do you remember whether when you attended as a witness on the first occasion as part of the Defence case in November 2000, whether Mr. Harmon suggested to you at all that you had attended a meeting of the 12th of July and not the 11th, or whether it was only on the second occasion when you came back?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon always asserted I did not attended that meeting on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I'm leaving that issue now and moving on to the second of the possibilities. Mr. Jevdjevic, on a scale of 1:10, where one means almost impossible to remember and 10 means utterly unforgettable, where would you place the 11th of July 1995 as a day in your life?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely as regards when I left the forward command post, where I went, what I saw, and the meeting that was held in the brigade command, absolutely all this is number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is there one per cent of one chance that you are wrong about the date on which you attended the meeting of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevdjevic. I am done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that -- Mr. Jevdjevic, you will be pleased to hear me say or confirm that your testimony ends here. You are free to go. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and stayed all these days with us giving evidence, and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. There is the long Miletic list which has been circulated. Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objections to that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. So they are all admitted. If there are any that still require translation, they will be MFI'd. Mr. Zivanovic, you don't have any documents do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is one e-court document. It is actually the map of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection from anyone? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it is admitted. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you give me a moment to catch up by going to Mr. McCloskey first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's been sent out. Ms. Stewart has sent it all out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not really an objection. It is about document P14, 14, the same document is on our list, 5D1412. What embarrasses me here with the document on e-court, on the list of the Prosecutor, is number P4094, which was the B/C/S version which doesn't completely correspond to the English version. And, in particular, for the last page of the document in e-court it has nothing to do with the document which concerns the -- the training course for snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey? Or will you see to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will just get together with her and sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better. I think it's better. Any further -- otherwise there are no objections, I take it, from anyone? All right. So the Prosecution list is also -- documents is also approved. They are admitted, saving what you need to discuss. Any -- yes, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is slightly belated, but there is an objection on our part to 5D1374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, 5D1374. Mainly this is a question of principle. The document was put to the witness, the witness didn't know anything about it, counsel moved on. That is not a submission basis for admission of the document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not a strictly common law jurisdiction. You know that. The way we proceed -- I mean, we are in a position then to decide whether to just ignore the document or -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think it's important to the credibility of the witnesses sometimes when he -- or a witness may particularly remember lots about lots of details and then suddenly doesn't know something about something significant. I think that's something you could take into consideration in a particular context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in the realm of admissibility only here. So anything else? We still have not got -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got one document. In fact, Your Honours, if I may make a correction. On the list that we provided, there are two documents, but only one was shown to the document -- to the witness. So we are only seeking to tender 6D328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we are anxious to know if anyone is taking a point on that document bearing in mind what was said when it was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you will soon know. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before I get into that particular area, I would like to just make -- refer the Court to one thing. There was a cross-examination on my questioning regarding the frequency, and my suggestion that roughly half or over half the majority of our documents were from that frequency. And I wanted to direct the Court's attention to Mr. Pajic's testimony at page 2882 where, when he was testifying, he said that: "These frequencies weren't changed, and that was the case until the end of the war. If there were any disturbances, one would go a megahertz up or down." So my factual conclusion when I asked that question was - and suggested that - a majority of our intercepts came within that particular frequency, I was including a megahertz up or down based on his answer. I could have formed the question more clearly so that would have been clear, but I did not; and I think Mr. Zivanovic was correct in pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, any objections to Mr. Josse's proposed exhibit, 6D328?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We would like time to investigate this further. These are significant documents. We have heard that the story where they came from. It is apparent to us, as they told us, that there are more documents from this source, and they have chosen not to provide us with any of those documents. And so in always in looking at the authenticity of a document, if you can have the other source document that came from the same source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it's a very good idea to have those. We were not given those, so we would like a chance to look into this document, and if we could treat it maybe like we treat the translation issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we MFI it for the time being and then you will let us know in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose there is much I can say about that save for the fact that we had the original in court. It's no longer here; it's on its way back to Serbia, as I understand it. But it was here available to the Prosecution to look at, and that's one of the reasons why I am only putting 328 in, because that's the one that was the original. So if it's being suggested that that document that was shown to the witness is not authentic, that really is the only question in my submission, this Chamber should asks ask itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. McCloskey, he's not saying that. He just wants to make a find out, and then he will tell us later if he still objects to this document or not and on what basis on that case. That's how I understand him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the Chamber thinks that's reasonable, then I am not going to stand in the way. The only thing about it is this: If there is some challenge to its authenticity, then I accept we need to prove it; and we need to make arrangements to do just that which requires effort and work on our part which we will do if need be. However, I repeat, the purported original was here for him and his team to inspect; he chose not to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.text: Anyway, thank you. We will await for a feedback on this from you, Mr. McCloskey, after your consultations with Mr. Haynes. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand the issue, the question was whether or not P210 as proffered by the Prosecution, you wanted us to address its relevance pursuant to Rule 89(c) and the question of potential prejudice to the Defence in terms of the administration of a fair trial under Rule 89(d). There are several reasons why we believe that this evidence is particularly relevant in the circumstances. For the sake of brevity, I think I will address the most obvious one first; and that has to do with the Defence submissions as derived from their opening statement. And in particular in respect of their submission that at the time that Mr. Borovcanin returns to Bratunac - and this is at page 26642 of the transcript - that at the time he returns to Bratunac and he assumes command of the units that are assigned to him, that he has no choice but to rely on the VRS commander in whose area of responsibility he is assigned for logistical support, security support, and perhaps most importantly for information. And the reason why I raise this first is that what P210 establishes is that Borovcanin, when he returns to Bratunac, is not returning in a space of a vacuum. He is returning to Bratunac to an area that he's familiar with, to individuals which he's familiar with, that are part of the political -- part of the political leadership of the municipality. What P210 shows is that his association with the SDS is directly related to this issue. He arrives with contacts in the political establishment of Bratunac municipality, will show his affiliation and association with memberships, with the membership of that leadership. The Defence's claim therefore, in our view, opens the door to these associations, the nature and the extent of the associations, and his ability to gain information other than the information which the Defence has argued. He is bound or constrained to rely on only emanating from the source of the VRS commander in the area. Clearly, the question of Mr. Borovcanin's associations with members of the political leadership, membership -- members of the SDS, in Bratunac in 1995 is responsive to this particular issue. Secondarily, his association with the SDS and the political leadership in Bratunac is relevant to the question of character which was specifically raised during the course of the opening statement - and that's at page 26654 of the transcript, where Mr. Gosnell says explicitly: "You are going to hear and read evidence of the good character of Mr. Borovcanin." And we are all familiar with the basic rules as concerns the use of character evidence in criminal cases, but, fundamentally, the chief concern with respect to the consideration of such character evidence has to do with the potential to conflate the evidence that's used to rebut the character evidence that's proffered with the crimes that are charged in the case; in other words, that there might be some confusion that may arises as a result of considering those underlying bad acts, uncharged crimes in the context of the crimes charged. What we propose here is that the evidence is relevant to the extent -- what this -- well, the evidence in this case relates specifically to his association with members of the SDS. It goes to his closeness to the membership -- to the members of that organisation, it goes to the strength of his ties, to the key players in the political group, and it also goes to his association with members of the organisation whom we know - and whom the evidence establishes - have a clear record of criminality as concerns conduct during the course of the war; specifically, Miroslav Deronjic and Radovan Karadzic. Miroslav Deronjic, in fact, was said to have been a close friend of the witness who testified, Ljubisav Simic, in this case. And he was said to have taken care of the party about the quality composition of the membership of the party, et cetera; and that and P210 specifically relates to the witness's function in that respect and also establishes the ties, that we submit, Mr. Borovcanin has to the organisation and the individual members of the organisation that reflect on his character directly. And, in fact, Radovan Karadzic, as you know, is alleged to have been a member of the JCE -- both JCEs that are alleged in the indictment in this case. He obviously has very close ties to Miroslav Deronjic, who was the sponsor, at least according to the document, of Mr. Borovcanin's membership. For these reasons and the more clear reasons that have to do with the credibility of the witness, we submit that this evidence is clearly relevant and probative. The question as to whether or not it imposes any undue hardship or undue prejudice to Defence on 89(d) so as to effect the administration of a fair trial is a slightly different issue; but it relates to the Defence's decision to put forward a case and to put forward evidence to which this document directly responds. I think I will cut it short there since we are just about out of time. I want to give my colleague a chance to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I suppose I start in auspiciously having been just several minutes ago reminded that this is a hybrid Tribunal in which the concepts expressed in the rules must be applied flexibly, and certainly that's an important thing for all of us to remember. But nonetheless, every legal system, civil law or common law, is modelled on a certain progression of presentation of charges, presentation of Prosecution evidence, presentation of Defence evidence, and once that evidence is actually created, a submission of arguments based on that evidence which has been presented in a certain fashion. And Rule 89(c) is one piece of a larger structure of the rules that in fact embodies that progression. And if he start to deviate from that progression in various ways by saying, Well these concepts are flexible, they can be applied in different ways and different circumstances, that's fine for individual cases as long as we preserve that progression and that notion of orderliness. So what I am appealing to you, Your Honours, to remember or to bear in mind in addressing this issue is that there is a larger question of ordinariness at steak. And frankly, Your Honours, I expected the submissions of the Prosecution to be somewhat more anodyne and pedestrian than what I heard, because what I heard quite frankly was an amend the indictment. One of the key arguments that was just presented my friend is that now, I learn, that Mr. Borovcanin is alleged to be involved in some kind of a JCE with the political leadership in Bratunac. That was the essential argument being presented by my friend opposite. Now, this is nowhere to be found in the indictment and it's nowhere to be found for that matter, at least in terms of any explicit fashion, in the Prosecution evidence presented during its case. And this is the kind of thing that is precisely what prejudices the fair trial of my client. It's the introduction of this kind of argumentation without having proper notice that this is what is being charged, that these are the mechanisms by which a crime in which my client allegedly participated are being presented. This is at the essence of what prejudices a fair defence. Now, to be quite honest with you, Mr. President, we think that we have done a very good job of showing that what was alleged during the cross-examination of the witness was utterly unfounded. That the document does not show that the my client was a part of the SDS, that he was not part of some cabal of individuals that were engaged in some parallel structure of any kind. We think we have shown that quite well. But the principle is important. Allowing the Prosecution to introduce these new elements is dangerous for the progression, the orderly progression of the trial. And it's primarily on that base that we assert that Rule 89(c) has not been satisfied. Because the question or the conditions that are set by Rule 89(c) is that there must be relevant evidence that has probative value. Relevant to what and probative of what? And that's where the charges in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief and in the Prosecution case are concerned. That's the benchmark against which they are presenting their evidence. Now, just to take the second point, moving on from the political leadership argument, the second point being this character evidence argument. Your Honours, we are in a non-bifurcating structure where we must present character evidence in relation to the accused to the extent that you are consider it in sentencing. Is the Prosecution now suggesting that if we present character evidence for any purpose that now means that they can present all manner of character evidence which - according to my learned friend - essentially comes down to, he was associating with bad people whom they identify as the SDS. This is the kind of thing, that frankly is beneath the dignity, I think, of the Bench. It leads to swelling of submissions in the final briefs. It leads to the Chamber being flooded with all kinds of arguments on essentially extraneous issues. And this is the kind of issue that really burdens the Chamber and slows down the progress of the trial. Mr. President, subject to any questions you may have, those are my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The -- yes, Mr. Gosnell. At the risk of evaporation. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we are handing now an oral decision both as regards this document and the other one, which was - correct me if I am wrong - 383, I think its P383.

Having said that, before we wind up ten minutes after schedule, may I, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, first of all thank you all, not only Prosecution and Defence, but all our precious staff, in the courtroom and behind the dark windows. I was approached yesterday by one of you, who said maybe you have never seen me, but I am helping from behind the stained windows. We appreciate very much all that you have done throughout these months that we have been sitting after the last recess. It has been a long session. I want you to believe me when I say that we really appreciate all your efforts. And before we all leave this courtroom for the recess, I wish to wish you all and your representative loved ones and family, all the very best for this festive season and for the new year which will, hopefully, see the end of this trial. Have a great time, enjoy yourself, relax, and rest as much as you can because still the journey is long haired, and we have still got months and months to work together. So happy Christmas and happy new year to all of you.
